How many days a year do trees have leaves?

The average time from spring leaf-out to autumn leaf drop, everywhere in the lower 48 states at 800-meter detail. Built from forest-canopy cameras and 30 years of climate normals. Hover the map, tap a spot, or search for a town.

    Reference cities

    Values at each city's location on the map. Select a row to show it on the map; select a column heading to sort.

    How this map was made

    The question, per spot: find the average date leaves start growing, find the average date they are down, and count the days in between. Leaf-out here is when a forest canopy first shows 10% of its summer green; leaf drop is when it is 90% of the way back to bare (leaves fallen or fully browned).

    Ground truth: the PhenoCam Network photographs forest canopies every half hour. At about 140 deciduous-forest cameras across the country, I averaged each site's yearly leaf-out and leaf-drop dates over its record (2008–2025).

    The model: leaves come out once enough spring warmth accumulates, and trees that had a colder winter need less warmth (a chill-adjusted degree-day model). Leaves drop once cool weather and shortening days add up past a threshold (the Delpierre model). Both were fit to the camera dates, then run on PRISM 1991–2020 day-by-day temperature normals for all 12 million 800-meter grid cells (800 m monthly averages, shaped day by day with PRISM's 4 km daily normals).

    Why Miami is year-round: in South Florida it never gets cool enough for leaves to drop, so the model keeps them on all year, matching the region's mostly evergreen trees. Florida citizen-science records from USA-NPN agree with the model's mid-February leaf-out and late-January leaf drop for central Florida.

    The half-year line marks where trees have leaves exactly half the year (182 days). East of the Rockies it runs from Colorado's Front Range across central Nebraska and Iowa, through Chicago, across northern Ohio and central Pennsylvania, to Connecticut and Rhode Island. North of it, and higher up, trees are bare more of the year than they are leafy. In the West, elevation matters more than latitude, so the line loops around the mountain ranges, where trees are bare most of the year.

    Limits: this is the season for deciduous trees on typical sites. Evergreen trees (pines, firs, live oaks) keep leaves all year everywhere. City trees often hold leaves 1–2 weeks longer than nearby forests, oak forests later than maple and aspen forests, and desert trees can drop leaves early in drought.

    Sources: PhenoCam Network transition dates (phenocam.nau.edu); PRISM Climate Group, Oregon State University, 1991–2020 normals (800 m monthly, 4 km daily); USA National Phenology Network spring index and Nature's Notebook observations; US Census Bureau 2023 gazetteer and population estimates. Map projection: US Albers equal-area.
